rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Before Islam, people without a borrowed garment circumambulated naked; garments discarded afterward could not be touched, a practice called liqāʾ.
rows.anchor: من لم يكن له صديق بمكة يعيره ثوبا طاف عريانا أو في ثيابه وألقاها بعد فلا يمسها أحد ويسمى اللقاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poet lamented the discarded garment as exposed among pilgrims, and a woman recited that what appeared of her body was forbidden to others.
rows.anchor: كفى حزنا كري عليه كأنه ...

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In year nine, the Prophet's proclamation barred polytheists from pilgrimage and naked circumambulation after the command to take adornment at every mosque.
rows.anchor: وكان النداء بمكة سنة تسع،

rows.speaker: عطاء وأبو روق
rows.claim: They explain adornment as grooming and combing the beard.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء وأبو روق: تسريح اللحى

rows.speaker: الماوردي
rows.claim: He explains adornment as wearing one's finest clothes at Friday prayers and festivals.
rows.anchor: وقيل: التزين بأجمل اللباس في الجمع والأعياد ذكره الماوردي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other reported meanings include lifting the hands in prayer, congregational mosque prayer, and praying in sandals; Ibn Atiyya doubts the sandal report.
rows.anchor: وقيل إقامة الصلاة في الجماعة بالمساجد وكان ذلك زينة لهم

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Adornment includes covering clothes, Friday perfume, siwak, fresh clothes, and any religiously approved beautification without vanity; covering nakedness is central at prayer.
rows.anchor: الزينة هنا الثياب الساترة ويدخل فيها ما كان من الطيب للجمعة والسواك وبدل الثياب

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He takes adornment as clothing and finery worn for each prayer, noting that people had circumambulated naked.
rows.anchor: خذوا زينتكم أي ريشكم ولباس زينتكم عند كل مسجد كلما صليتم وكانوا يطوفون عراة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adornment means what beautifies a worshipper; the command cannot mean only covering nakedness, which is required generally and is not specific to prayer at every mosque.
rows.anchor: والذي يظهر أن الزينة هو ما يتجمل به ويتزين عند الصلاة ولا يدخل فيه ما يستر العورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Restricting the general command to covering nakedness during circumambulation would oddly narrow a general address to those at the one specific sanctuary.
rows.anchor: وتقييد الأمر بما يستر العورة في الطواف مفض إلى تخصيصه بمن يطوف بالبيت

rows.speaker: أبو بكر الرازي
rows.claim: He treats the verse as proof that covering nakedness is obligatory in prayer, citing Abu Yusuf, Zufar, Muhammad, al-Hasan ibn Ziyad, and al-Shafiʿi.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو بكر الرازي في الآية دليل على فرض ستر العورة في الصلاة وهو قول أبي يوسف وزفر ومحمد

rows.speaker: مالك والليث
rows.claim: They hold that exposing nakedness is forbidden and recommend repeating a prayer performed uncovered within its time.
rows.anchor: كشف العورة حرام ويوجبان الإعادة في الوقت

rows.speaker: الأبهري
rows.claim: He says covering is obligatory in general, in prayer and elsewhere; the author endorses this as correct, citing the Prophet's instruction not to walk naked.
rows.anchor: وقال الأبهري: هي فرض في الجملة وعلى الإنسان أن يسترها في الصلاة وغيرها وهو الصحيح

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: He says the command permits meat, fat, and milk, which people had forbidden themselves during ihram.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: معناه كلوا من اللحم والدسم واشربوا من الألبان

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: He identifies the permitted food with the bahīra and related livestock that people had forbidden.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: كلوا من البحيرة وأخواتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording generally permits all foods and drinks lawful under the religion, even if the revelation arose from a narrower pagan restriction.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه أمر بإباحة الأكل والشرب من كل ما يمكن أن يؤكل أو يشرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibition of extravagance is a prohibition, since God says He does not love those who exceed bounds.
rows.anchor: والنهي عن الإسراف يدل على التحريم لقوله إنه لا يحب المسرفين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He defines extravagance as departing from the middle course, and also as prohibiting what God made lawful.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: الإسراف الخروج عن حد الاستواء، وقال أيضا لا تسرفوا في تحريم ما أحل لكم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He says one may eat and dress freely so long as neither extravagance nor conceit is involved.
rows.anchor: كل ما شئت والبس ما شئت ما أخطأتك خصلتان سرف ومخيلة

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: He defines extravagance as eating what is forbidden.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد: الإسراف أكل الحرام

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: He defines extravagance as eating lawful food beyond one's need.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج الإسراف الأكل من الحلال فوق الحاجة

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: He interprets extravagance as associating partners with God.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: الإسراف الإشراك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation calls the pagans' clapping and whistling during naked circumambulation extravagance and disobedience.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الإسراف مخالفة أمر الله في طوافهم عراة يصفقون ويصفرون

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He also says lawful things contain no extravagance; extravagance lies in committing sins.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس أيضا: ليس في الحلال سرف إنما السرف في ارتكاب المعاصي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A story says a Christian physician at Hārūn al-Rashīd's court denied that scripture or the Prophet taught medicine; cited advice on eating and avoiding excess persuaded him otherwise.
rows.anchor: وحكى المفسرون هنا أن نصرانيا طبيبا للرشيد أنكر أن يكون في القرآن أو في حديث الرسول شيء من الطب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's adornment is what religious law approves for beautification, including clothing; it is attributed to God because He made it permissible.
rows.anchor: زينة الله ما حسنته الشريعة وقررته مما يتجمل به من الثياب وغيرها وأضيفت إلى الله لأنه هو الذي أباحها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The good provisions are pleasant foods and drinks that are lawful; another view simply defines them as permitted things.
rows.anchor: والطيبات هي المستلذات من المأكول والمشروب بطريقة وهو الحل،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question rebukes those who forbid good adornment and provisions, including the pagans' self-imposed bans on meat and milk.
rows.anchor: ومعنى الاستفهام إنكار تحريم هذه الأشياء وتوبيخ محرميها

rows.speaker: مكي
rows.claim: Makkī mistakenly takes the following words, “Say: they are,” as an answer to the rhetorical question; a denial-bearing question needs no answer.
rows.anchor: وتوهم مكي هنا أن له جوابا هنا وهو قوله قل هي توهم فاسد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He explains “brought forth” as making something manifest; another interpretation is distinguishing its lawful and unlawful forms.
rows.anchor: ومعنى أخرج أبرزها وأظهرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qatāda reads “for whoever believes”; Nāfiʿ reads “exclusive” nominative, while the other seven readers use the accusative.
rows.anchor: قرأ قتادة قل هي لمن آمن، وقرأ نافع خالصة بالرفع، وقرأ باقي السبعة بالنصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative can mark a circumstantial state: the adornment is available to believers in this life and reserved to them alone on Judgment Day; Ibn Jubayr reads this as freedom from punishment for enjoying it.
rows.anchor: فأما النصب فعلى الحال والتقدير قل هي مستقرة للذين آمنوا في حال خلوصها لهم يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “exclusive” may be a second predicate: adornment is shared in worldly life but continues exclusively for believers in Paradise, as Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Daḥḥāk, Qatāda, al-Ḥasan, Ibn Jurayj, and Ibn Zayd hold.
rows.anchor: أي قل هي كائنة في الحياة الدنيا للمؤمنين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والضحاك وقتادة والحسن وابن جريج وابن زيد
rows.claim: They say the adornment is shared by believers and unbelievers in this world, then exclusive to believers in the next.
rows.anchor: وهذا المعنى من أنها لهم ولغيرهم في الدنيا خالصة لهم يوم القيامة هو قول ابن عباس

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He explains that unbelievers share the adornment in this life, while it belongs exclusively to believers in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: وعلى هذا المعنى فسر الزمخشري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author endorses Ibn ʿAṭiyya’s warning: overspending on clothes until one’s wealth is exhausted leaves one’s family impoverished, a prohibited harmful excess.
rows.anchor: مثال ذلك أن يفرط في شراء ثياب أو نحوها ويستنفد في ذلك حل ماله

rows.speaker: الكرماني
rows.claim: He supplies an ellipsis: the adornment is for believers and unbelievers in this world, exclusively for believers in the next life.
rows.anchor: أن في الكلام حذفا تقديره قل هي للمؤمنين والكافرين في الدنيا خالصة للمؤمنين في القيامة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He supplies an implied non-exclusive worldly share, since polytheists share the goods, while they are exclusive in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: قاله الزمخشري قال: قل هي للذين آمنوا في الحياة الدنيا غير خالصة لهم

rows.speaker: التبريزي
rows.claim: He says worldly goods are shared by the righteous and wicked but are attributed to believers as their primary creation; unbelievers are derivative users.
rows.anchor: قال التبريزي معنى الآية أنها للمؤمنين خالصة في الآخرة لا يشركهم الكفار فيها

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: He allows “in the life of this world” to attach to “forbidden,” while al-Akhfash allows it to attach to “brought forth.”
rows.anchor: وقال أبو علي في الحجة ويصح أن يعلق قوله في الحياة الدنيا بقوله حرم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He says Abu ʿAlī and al-Akhfash’s other attachments to “the good things” or “of provision” fragment the wording and harm its eloquence.
rows.anchor: ويصح أن يتعلق بقوله والطيبات ويصح أن يتعلق بقوله من الرزق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects the syntactic comparison with 10:27: there “a requital for an evil deed in kind” is the predicate, with “from them” understood, and “disgrace overtakes them” coordinates with it.
rows.anchor: بل قوله جزاء سيئة بمثلها هو خبر عن النهي أي جزاء سيئة منهم بمثلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God will continue to distinguish the signs for people with knowledge, since only the knowledgeable benefit from such explanation; he cites the parable understood only by the learned.
rows.anchor: مثل تفصيلنا وتقسيمنا السابق نقسم في المستقبل لقوم لهم علم وإدراك

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: After Muslims wore clothes and circumambulated, pagans reproached them for supposedly deeming the sacred precinct permissible; the verse was revealed in response.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي لما لبس المسلمون الثياب وطافوا بالبيت عيرهم المشركون بذلك

rows.speaker: التبريزي
rows.claim: He interprets open indecency as men's daytime naked circumambulation and hidden indecency as women's naked circumambulation at night.
rows.anchor: ما ظهر منها طواف الرجل بالنهار عريانا وما بطن طوافها بالليل عارية قاله التبريزي

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: He identifies public indecency with pagan naked circumambulation and hidden indecency with adultery.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: ما ظهر طواف الجاهلية عراة وما بطن الزنا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد
rows.claim: In one report, public indecency includes pre-Islamic incest and prohibited combinations of marriage; hidden indecency is adultery.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس ومجاهد في رواية: ما ظهر ما كانت تفعله الجاهلية من نكاح الأبناء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word “sin” broadly covers sinful speech and actions; others restrict it to minor sins or to wine, but he rejects the wine interpretation in this Meccan context.
rows.anchor: والإثم عام يشمل الأقوال والأفعال التي يترتب عليها الإثم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He says “sin” cannot mean wine here: the sura is Meccan, wine was prohibited only after Uḥud, and companions died as martyrs with it still in their bodies.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول لا يصح هنا لأن السورة مكية ولم تحرم الخمر إلا بالمدينة بعد أحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse “I drank sin until my mind departed” is fabricated; if sound, it would mean the cause of sin, not wine itself.
rows.anchor: وهو بيت مصنوع مختلق وإن صح فهو على حذف مضاف أي موجب الإثم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن
rows.claim: They are reported to have called wine sin; the author says this could name the cause by its effect.
rows.anchor: ولا يذل قول ابن عباس والحسن الإثم الخمر على أنه من أسمائها

rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: He denies that sin is a name for wine.
rows.anchor: وأنكر أبو العباس أن يكون الإثم من أسماء الخمر

rows.speaker: الفضل
rows.claim: He identifies sin with wine and adduces a poem as evidence.
rows.anchor: وقال الفضل: الإثم الخمر، وأنشد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author notes that wine may be called sin and cites a poem using the term for wine.
rows.anchor: قال: وقد تسمى الخمر إثما وأنشد: شربت الإثم حتى زل عقلي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والفراء
rows.claim: They define transgression as overreaching or acting arrogantly.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس والفراء: البغي الاستطالة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: He interprets transgression as intoxication from any drink.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: السكر من كل شراب

rows.speaker: ثعلب
rows.claim: He defines it as speaking about someone unjustly, except when responding with a rightful defense.
rows.anchor: وقال ثعلب: تكلم الرجل في الرجل بغير الحق إلا أن ينتصر منه بحق

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He defines transgression as injustice and arrogance.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الظلم والكبر، قاله الزمخشري

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Transgression is exceeding limits, whether one initiates it or retaliates.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: البغي التعدي وتجاوز الحد مبتدئا كان أو منتصرا

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Transgression is exceeding limits, whether one initiates it or retaliates; “without right” clarifies, since a rightful act is not transgression.
rows.anchor: البغي التعدي وتجاوز الحد مبتدئا كان أو منتصرا وقوله بغير الحق زيادة بيان

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He calls the wording about lacking revealed authority a taunt, since no proof could authorize associating partners with God.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري فيه تهكم لأنه لا يجوز أن ينزل برهانا بأن يشرك به غيره

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He says the forbidden assertion is that angels are God's daughters.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس أراد بذلك أن الملائكة بنات الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation is the pagans' invented prohibitions on foods, clothing, and drinks during ihram.
rows.anchor: قولهم أنه حرم عليهم مآكل وملابس ومشارب في الإحرام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse warns Meccans that, like earlier peoples, their punishment has a fixed time known to God if they disobey their Lord.
rows.anchor: هذا وعيد لأهل مكة بالعذاب النازل في أجل معلوم عند الله كما نزل بالأمم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other interpretations take each nation's appointed term as its worldly life span, after which it meets the record of its true or false deeds.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الأجل هنا أجل الدنيا التقدير: للأمم كلها أجل

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: He says “community” here means a faction or group, a word commonly used for many people.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: أي فرقة وجماعة وهي لفظة تستعمل في الكثير من الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another definition allows a community to be small or large, even a single person, as in the report about Quss ibn Sāʿida being raised alone as a community.
rows.anchor: والأمة الجماعة قلوا أو كثروا وقد يطلق على الواحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term “term” is singular because it is a generic noun, communities of an era have similar deeds, or the phrase means one term for every individual.
rows.anchor: وأفرد الأجل لأنه اسم جنس أو لتقارب أعمال أهل كل عصر أو لكون التقدير لكل واحد من أمة

rows.speaker: الحسن وابن سيرين
rows.claim: They read the word for appointed terms in the plural.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وابن سيرين فإذا جاء آجالهم بالجمع

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He explains “an hour” as the shortest time in ordinary speech, meaning the nearest or briefest moment.
rows.anchor: وقال ساعة لأنها أقل الأوقات في استعمال الناس يقول المستعجل لصاحبه في ساعة

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: He says “hour” denotes a small unit of time while intending the totality of its parts.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية لفظ عني به الجزء القليل من الزمان والمراد جمع أجزائه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A future negative after “when” may answer it with or without a prefixed fāʾ; without it, an omitted subject makes the response nominal, which requires fāʾ or sudden idhā.
rows.anchor: والمضارع المنفي بلا إذا وقع في الظاهر جوابا لإذا يجوز أن يتلقى بفاء الجزاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ḥawfī's coordination of “nor do they precede” with “they do not lag” fails: a future event cannot determine that a past event did not precede it, as the Zuhayr poem illustrates.
rows.anchor: وهذا لا يمكن لأن إذا شرطية فالذي يترتب عليها إنما هو مستقبل ولا يترتب على مجيء الأجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address is to the children of Adam; it may concern the primordial covenant or be framed as future at revelation to support the truth of Muhammad's prophethood.
rows.anchor: هذا الخطاب لبني آدم. قيل: هو في الأول

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: He says the emphatic nūn cannot enter without the conditional particle mā; some grammarians allow it.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية وإذا لم يكن ما لم يجز دخول النون الثقيلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The answer may be the conditional clause “whoever is God-fearing and reforms,” with “no fear” as its result; alternatively, “whoever” is relative and both believer and denier outcomes answer the first condition together.
rows.anchor: وجواب الشرط فمن اتقى فيحتمل أن تكون من شرطية وجوابه فلا خوف وتكون هذه الجملة الشرطية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God-fearing and reform presuppose faith, since without it conduct would lead to immersion in corruption rather than reform.
rows.anchor: وتضمن قوله فمن اتقى وأصلح سبق الإيمان إذ لا ينشأ عنه إلا الانهماك والإفساد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believer's reform contrasts with the deniers' arrogance: good action follows piety, while arrogance follows rejecting revelation and prevents obedience to messengers.
rows.anchor: وقابل الإصلاح بالاستكبار لأن إصلاح العمل من نتيجة التقوى والاستكبار من نتيجة التكذيب

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: He says those who reject a messenger either sincerely believe him false or arrogantly deny him without firm conviction, the latter being unbelief out of defiance.
rows.anchor: إما أن يكذب بحسب اعتقاده أنه كذب وإما أن يستكبر فيكذب وإن كان غير مصمم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clauses omit a connective pronoun understood as “among you” in both the pious and the deniers' descriptions.
rows.anchor: وتضمنت الجملتان حذف رابط وتقديره فمن اتقى وأصلح منكم، والذين كذبوا منكم

rows.speaker: أبي والأعرج
rows.claim: They read the verb “come” in the feminine, with “recount” agreeing by sense with the plural group rather than grammatical form.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبي والأعرج إما تأتينكم بالتاء على تأنيث الجماعة ويقصون محمول على المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He reads “nor do they precede” as a new report that people do not get ahead of their appointed term; together the clauses deny both preceding and delaying it.
rows.anchor: والذي تخرج عليه الآية أن قوله ولا يستقدمون منقطع من الجواب على سبيل استئناف إخبار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After mentioning deniers, the text names those even worse: people who invent lies about God as well as reject His signs.
rows.anchor: لما ذكر المكذبين ذكر أسوأ حالا منهم وهو من يفتري الكذب على الله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وابن جبير ومجاهد
rows.claim: They interpret the allotted portion of scripture as each person's written happiness or misery; the author says this does not fit what follows.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس وابن جبير ومجاهد: ما كتب لهم من السعادة والشقاوة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: He takes their allotted portion to mean the punishment written for them.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: ما كتب لهم من العذاب

rows.speaker: الربيع ومحمد بن كعب وابن زيد
rows.claim: They explain it as what was decreed for them in the primordial register.
rows.anchor: وقال الربيع ومحمد بن كعب وابن زيد: ما سبق لهم في أم الكتاب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة
rows.claim: They say it is what the recording angels wrote in people's books of deeds, namely their disbelief and sins.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس أيضا ومجاهد أيضا وقتادة: ما كتب الحفظة في صحائف الناس من الخير والشر

rows.speaker: الحكم وأبو صالح
rows.claim: They define the portion as worldly provision, life spans, good, and evil allotted to people.
rows.anchor: وقال الحكم وأبو صالح ما كتب لهم من الأرزاق والأعمار والخير والشر في الدنيا

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: He interprets it as the reward and punishment written for them.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك: ما كتب لهم من الثواب والعقاب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والضحاك ومجاهد
rows.claim: They also interpret the written portion as people's disbelief and sins.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس أيضا والضحاك أيضا ومجاهد ما كتب لهم من الكفر والمعاصي

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Another report from him says it is their written misguidance and guidance.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن أيضا: ما كتب لهم من الضلالة والهدى

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another view from him says it means the deeds written for them.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس أيضا: ما كتب لهم من الأعمال

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد والضحاك
rows.claim: They take “from the Book” to mean the Qur'an and their share as blackened faces on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس ومجاهد والضحاك: من الكتاب يراد به من القرآن وحظهم فيه سواد وجوههم يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations are the preservation of a treaty granted upon payment of jizya or what the Preserved Tablet records, whose legal allotment is punishment and wrath.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ما أوجب من حفظ عهودهم إذا أعطوا الجزية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He prefers the portion allotted in worldly life, such as provision and term, since the passage culminates with “until” their death; al-Zamakhsharī takes this similarly as provisions and deeds.
rows.anchor: والذي يظهر أن الذي كتب لهم في الدنيا من رزق وأجل وغيرهما ينالهم فيها ولذلك جاءت التغيية بعد هذا بحتى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects the claim that until here is merely an initial genitive particle; it expresses an endpoint.
rows.anchor: ووقع في التحرير حتى هنا ليس بغاية بل هي ابتداء وجر والجملة بعدها في موضع جر وهذا وهم

rows.speaker: ابن درستويه والزجاج
rows.claim: They say introductory until is a preposition, with its following clause in the genitive and related to what precedes.
rows.anchor: قولان: الأول لابن درستويه والزجاج، والثاني للجمهور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poem uses until to mark the endpoint at which mounts tire and horses can no longer be led by reins.
rows.anchor: سريت بهم حتى تكل مطيهم

rows.speaker: ابن درستويه والزجاج
rows.claim: Another poem uses until for the endpoint at which blood darkens the water of the Tigris.
rows.anchor: فما زالت القتلى تمج دماءها

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: They deny that introductory “until” is a preposition or syntactically governed by what precedes, though it retains an endpoint meaning.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: وهي حتى التي يبتدأ بعدها الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels question the dying about their supposed gods to rebuke them; they reply that the gods vanished, perished, or took another way.
rows.anchor: فيسألونهم سؤال توبيخ وتقرير أين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The usual interpretation is that messengers are the Angel of Death and his helpers, taking souls at death; “taking them” is circumstantial, and the relative mā should have been written separately.
rows.anchor: والرسل ملك الموت وأعوانه، ويتوفونهم في موضع الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “You call upon” may mean seeking the idols' help to fulfill needs.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معنى تدعون أي تستغيثونهم لقضاء حوائجكم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: An alternate group including al-Ḥasan identifies the messengers as angels of punishment on Judgment Day; “take them” means fully count them while driving them to Hell.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة منهم الحسن: الرسل ملائكة العذاب يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the Judgment Day reading, the allotted portion comes only then; a worldly allotment would have ended long before the stated endpoint.
rows.anchor: ونيل النصيب على هذا إنما هو في الآخرة إذ لو كان في الدنيا لما تحققت الغاية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “They confessed” may continue the disbelievers' answer or be God's separate report of their confession; this does not conflict with another group denying association in 6:23.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون استئناف إخبار من الله تعالى بإقرارهم على أنفسهم بالكفر ولا تعارض بين هذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though asked where the idols are, they answer that the idols are gone; this answers the implied question of what became of their gods.
rows.anchor: وجواب سؤالهم ليس مطابقا من جهة اللفظ لأنه سؤال عن مكان،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's command to enter with earlier communities addresses the Arab disbelievers; past tense signals certainty, and the words are spoken through angels.
rows.anchor: أي يقول الله لهم أي لكفار العرب وهم المفترون الكذب والمكذبون بالآيات وذلك يوم القيامة وعبر بالماضي لتحقق وقوعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Among communities” may attach to “enter” to mean in company, or be an omitted circumstantial clause; “passed before you” may mean earlier in life or earlier entering Hell.
rows.anchor: ويتعلق في أمم في الظاهر بادخلوا والمعنى في جملة أمم ويحتمل أن يتعلق بمحذوف فيكون في موضع الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jinn are named first because they lead in misleading others; the verse indicates that sinful jinn enter the Fire.
rows.anchor: وقدم الجن لأنهم الأصل في الإغواء والإضلال ودل ذلك على أن عصاة الجن يدخلون النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “In the Fire” may modify “passed before,” describe prior communities, or modify “enter” with “among communities” as company and “in the Fire” as location; apposition may license both prepositions.
rows.anchor: وفي النار متعلق بخلت على أن المعنى تقدم دخولها أو بمحذوف وهو صفة لأمم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Whenever” marks repeated entry; a later community curses an earlier one, or members of one entering group curse each other; sisterhood means shared religion.
rows.anchor: كلما للتكرار ولا يستوي ذلك في الأمة الأولى فالاحقة تلعن السابقة أو يلعن بعض الأمة الداخلة بعضها

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He defines the cursed “sister” as the community led astray by imitating the earlier one.
rows.anchor: أختها التي ضلت بالاقتداء بها انتهى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage describes the people of Hell cursing and opposing one another, as other verses also depict.
rows.anchor: والمعنى أن أهل النار يلعن بعضهم بعضا ويعادي بعضهم بعضا ويكفر بعضهم ببعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The successive communities curse one another until all have caught up and assembled in Hell; “until” completes the preceding sequence.
rows.anchor: حتى غاية لما قبلها والمعنى أنهم يدخلون فوجا ففوجا لاعنا بعضهم بعضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The form “they all caught up” derives from “they followed one another,” assimilating tāʾ into dāl and adding a connecting hamza.
rows.anchor: وأصل اداركوا تداركوا أدغمت التاء في الدال فاجتلبت همزة الوصل

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: He reads with a cut hamza; Abū al-Fatḥ calls this problematic and says it is a pause of surprise followed by a new start.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو عمرو واداركوا بقطع ألف الوصل، قال أبو الفتح

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: He reads with a cut alif, silent dāl, and open rāʾ, meaning that some caught others.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مجاهد بقطع الألف وسكون الدال وفتح الراء بمعنى أدرك بعضهم بعضا

rows.speaker: حميد
rows.claim: He reads the passive form, meaning that they were made to enter its realization.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حميد أدركوا بضم الهمزة وكسر الراء أي أدخلوا في إدراكها

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود والأعمش
rows.claim: They read “they followed one another”; the reading is also transmitted from Abū ʿAmr.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن مسعود والأعمش تداركوا ورويت عن أبي عمر

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: He records a reading with a single silent alif and doubled dāl, permitting two adjacent quiescent letters across a word boundary as in “the straying ones.”
rows.anchor: وقرىء إذا اداركوا بألف واحدة ساكنة والدال بعدها مشددة وهو جمع بين ساكنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Their last” may mean the latest followers who institutionalized error versus its first originators, low-ranking followers versus leaders, or those entering Hell last versus first; the last distinction is attributed to Muqātil.
rows.anchor: أخراهم الأمة الأخيرة في الزمان التي وجدت ضلالات مقررة مستعملة لأولاهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He says it means the final community addressing the first; “last” is the feminine counterpart of “first.”
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: آخر أمة لأول أمة وأخرى هنا بمعنى آخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām in “because of their first” denotes cause, since the later group addresses God, not its predecessors; its accusation says the leaders initiated or compelled its error and deserve extra punishment.
rows.anchor: واللام في لأولاهم لام السبب أي لأجل أولاهم لأن خطابهم مع الله لا معهم أضلونا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Each group receives a double punishment, but the first receives further endless increase because every torment is followed by another.
rows.anchor: أي لكل من الأخرى والأولى عذاب وللأولى عذاب متضاعف زائد إلى غير نهاية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers use the second-person plural: either God addresses the petitioners about each group's amount or description, or people in this world about its magnitude.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور بالتاء على الخطاب للسائلين أي لا تعلمون ما لكل فريق من العذاب

rows.speaker: أبو بكر والمفضل عن عاصم
rows.claim: They read the verb in third person; it may report the later community or both groups, each unaware of its own or the other's allotted punishment.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو بكر والمفضل عن عاصم بالياء فيحتمل أن يكون إخبارا عن الأمة

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: A report from him identifies the “double” as serpents and snakes.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن مسعود أن الضعف هنا الأفاعي والحيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's reply refuses the later group's request to increase its predecessors' torment.
rows.anchor: وهذه الجملة رد على أولئك السائلين وعدم إسعاف لما طلبوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The leaders tell their followers that following them gave no advantage or lighter punishment; Mujāhid specifically explains “advantage” as mitigation.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: معنى من فضل من التخفيف لما قال الله لكل ضعف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He reads “you had no advantage over us” as denying that following leaders made followers better: they chose unbelief freely rather than being forced.
rows.anchor: بل كفرتم اختيارا لا إنا حملناكم على ذلك إجبارا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He coordinates their statement with God's preceding declaration that each group has a double punishment; the author prefers an omitted preceding clause about their appeal to God.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: عطفوا هذا الكلام على قول الله تعالى للسلفة لكل ضعف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He takes “taste the punishment” as the leaders' gloating words to their followers, whose torment is for their own sins; another view makes God the speaker to all.
rows.anchor: وأن قوله فذوقوا العذاب من كلام الأولى خطابا للأخرى على سبيل التشفي منهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He says heaven's gates do not open to their deeds, prayers, or acts meant to obey God, contrasting the ascent of good words and deeds and the record of the righteous.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس لا تفتح لأعمالهم ولا لدعائهم ولا لما يريدون به طاعة الله تعالى

rows.speaker: السدي وغيره
rows.claim: They say heaven's gates do not open for the unbelievers' souls; reports distinguish the permission granted to a believer's soul from the rejection of a disbeliever's.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي وغيره: لا تفتح لأرواحهم وذكروا في صعود الروحين إلى السماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other readings place the closed gates at resurrection, barring entry to Paradise, or interpret them as withholding blessing and rain.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المعنى لا تفتح لهم أبواب السماء في القيامة ليدخلوا منها إلى الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers differ on the verb: Abū ʿAmr has light feminine tāʾ, the two imams light yāʾ, most of the seven doubled upper tāʾ, and Abū Ḥaywa and Abū al-Barr Haytham read doubled thāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو لا تفتح بتاء التأنيث والتخفيف، وقرأ الأخوان بالياء والتخفيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A camel passing through a needle's eye is an impossible endpoint, meaning they will never enter Paradise; the camel's size contrasts with the needle's tiny opening.
rows.anchor: والمعنى أنهم لا يدخلون الجنة أبدا،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poetry compares the camel's immense body with the needle-eye's narrowness and also uses the needle's eye as an image for the tightest passage.
rows.anchor: وذكر الجمل لأنه أعظم الحيوان المزاول للإنسان جثة فلا يلج إلا في باب واسع

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A widespread alternative reading, transmitted through Shahr ibn Ḥawshab and others, has a doubled mīm and means a thick ship's cable made by twisting ropes together.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عباس فيما روى عنه شهر بن حوشب ومجاهد وابن يعمر وأبو مجلز

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report, which the author says may be unsound, rejects comparing God to a camel and says the rope better fits a needle's eye.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن عباس ولعله لا يصح أن الله أحسن تشبيها من أن يشبه بالجمل

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: He says an Arabic reader of Ibn ʿAbbās's reading was non-Arab and doubled the jīm because of his language; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls this weak given its many transmitters.
rows.anchor: وعن الكسائي أن الذي روى الجمل عن ابن عباس كان أعجميا فشدد الجيم لعجمته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author reinforces the weakness objection by noting that readers beyond Ibn ʿAbbās also transmitted the reading.
rows.anchor: ولكثرة القراء بها غير ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Several variants attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās and others use different vowels or gemination for the cable reading, which variously denotes a thick ship's rope, coir cable, or palm-climbing rope.
rows.anchor: ومعناه في هذه القراءات الفلس الغليظ وهو حبل السفينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority's ordinary “camel” reading is more apt: the camel exemplifies huge size and the needle's eye extreme narrowness.
rows.anchor: وقراءة الجمهور الجمل بفتح الجيم الميم أوقع لأن سم الإبرة يضرب بها المثل في الضيق

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Asked what a camel is, he answers “the male of a she-camel,” exposing the questioner's ignorance rather than inventing another sense.
rows.anchor: وسئل ابن مسعود عن الجمل فقال زوج الناقة وذلك منه استجهال للسائل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers vary between a voiced and unvoiced sīn in “needle's eye,” and between kasra and fatḥa on the mīm of “needle.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله وقتادة وأبو رزين وابن مصرف وطلحة بضم سين سم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God requites criminals with the same sort of punishment; al-Zamakhsharī says criminality causes punishment and every criminal is punished, but the author detects a Muʿtazilite insinuation.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري ليؤذن أن الإجرام هو السبب الموصل إلى العقاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bedding and coverings are a metaphor for fire surrounding them on every side, as another verse describes fire-shadows above and below.
rows.anchor: هذه استعارة لما يحيط بهم من النار من كل جانب كما قال لهم من فوقهم ظلل من النار

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والقرظي وابن زيد
rows.claim: They explain the coverings as blankets; other reports call them smoke, a cover of fire, or bedding and blankets.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس والقرظي وابن زيد: هي اللحف

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: He defines the bedding as mattresses and the overhead coverings as quilts; grammarians debate whether the word's tanwīn compensates for a missing yāʾ or vowel.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك: المهاد الفرش والغواشي اللحف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After warning unbelievers, the passage promises believers Paradise; the exception about capacity may interrupt the predicate or form part of it, and shows righteous works are within reach.
rows.anchor: وفائدته أنه لما ذكر قوله وعملوا الصالحات نبه على أن ذلك العمل وسعهم وغير خارج عن قدرتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This also encourages unbelievers: despite Paradise's greatness, it can be reached through manageable deeds without hardship.
rows.anchor: وفيه تنبيه للكفار على أن الجنة مع عظم محالها يوصل إليها بالعمل السهل من غير مشقة

rows.speaker: القاضي أبو بكر بن الطيب
rows.claim: He says financial duties to wives extend only to what one possesses and can afford, not to establishing capacity before action; the author says the context does not support this reading.
rows.anchor: لم يكلف أحدا في نفقات الزوجات إلا ما وجد وتمكن منه دون ما لا تناله يده

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He reads the capacity clause as an interruption encouraging pursuit of the vast eternal reward through faith and good deeds; the author detects a Muʿtazilite implication.
rows.anchor: للترغيب في اكتساب ما لا يكتنهه وصف الواصف من النعيم الخالد

rows.speaker: الأعمش
rows.claim: He reads the verb without tāʾ: “no soul is burdened.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعمش لا تكلف نفس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Removing rancor means making Paradise's inhabitants free of grudges; another view specifically denies envy over their differing ranks.
rows.anchor: أي أذهبنا في الجنة ما انطوت عليه صدورهم من الحقود

rows.speaker: الحسن وسهل بن عبد الله
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan calls it rancor from the pre-Islamic period; Sahl calls it passions and innovations.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: غل الجاهلية، وقال سهل بن عبد الله الأهواء والبدع

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: A report from ʿAlī says the verse was revealed about the people of Badr; he hopes he, ʿUthmān, Ṭalḥa, and al-Zubayr are among them.
rows.anchor: وروي عن علي كرم الله وجهه فينا والله أهل بدر نزلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He takes the removal of rancor as a figure for God creating them with pure hearts, mutual affection, and love, like brothers facing one another on couches.
rows.anchor: والذي يظهر أن النزع للغل كناية عن خلقهم في الآخرة سالمي القلوب طاهريها متوادين متعاطفين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects taking “rivers flowing beneath them” as a circumstantial clause governed by “removed” or by an idāfa; it is an independent predicate describing their state.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه خبر مستأنف عن صفة حالهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people of Paradise praise God for enabling them to reach this great blessing through faith and righteous action.
rows.anchor: أي وفقنا لتحصيل هذا النعيم الذي صرنا إليه بالإيمان والعمل الصالح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other readings take guidance as showing them the road and their homes in Paradise, directing them to the righteous deed rewarded, or granting the faith that qualified them.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الهداية هنا هو الإرشاد إلى طريق الجنة ومنازلهم فيها

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He says God enabled them for the cause of their great triumph—faith and good works; the author flags the word “cause” as Muʿtazilite doctrine.
rows.anchor: أي وفقنا لموجب هذا الفوز العظيم وهو الإيمان والعمل الصالح

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: He explains guidance as God giving capacity together with decisive motivation, which jointly produce the virtue.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبد الله الرازي معنى هدانا الله أعطانا القدرة وضم إليها

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: They say praise is for God creating intellect, presenting proofs, and removing impediments.
rows.anchor: وقالت المعتزلة التحميد إنما وقع على أنه تعالى خلق العقل ووضع الدلائل وأزال الموانع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A sound Muslim report says Paradise's inhabitants will live forever, remain healthy and youthful forever, and never lose their bliss.
rows.anchor: إذا دخل أهل الجنة الجنة نادى مناد إن لكم أن تحيوا فلا تموتوا أبدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their statement that they would not have found guidance without God's guidance confirms that God creates their guidance and they could not have guided themselves.
rows.anchor: وهذه الجملة توضح أن الله خالق الهداية فيهم وأنهم لو خلوا وأنفسهم لم تكن منهم هداية

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He paraphrases the clause as saying they could not have been rightly guided without God's guidance and enabling grace.
rows.anchor: وما كان يستقيم أن نكون مهتدين لولا هداية الله تعالى وتوفيقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He prefers taking the clause after the waw as a new sentence, not a circumstantial clause; Ibn ʿĀmir's reading without waw likewise makes it explanatory.
rows.anchor: والثاني: أظهر. وقرأ ابن عامر ما كنا بغير واو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Basran grammar requires an omitted answer to the conditional lawlā: without God's guidance they would not have been guided or would have strayed; most Basrans do not allow an answer to precede its condition.
rows.anchor: والذي تقتضيه أصول العربية أن جواب لولا محذوف لدلالة ما قبله عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A sound Muslim report says no one enters Paradise by deeds alone, including the Prophet, unless God covers him with mercy and grace.
rows.anchor: لن يدخل الجنة أحد بعمله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people of Paradise's announcement is phrased in the past to assure its future fulfillment; it reproaches and rebukes the people of Hell.
rows.anchor: عبر بالماضي عن المستقبل لتحقق وقوعه وهذا النداء فيه تقريع وتوبيخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exchange heightens Hell's anguish because its inhabitants hear the announcement while Paradise's people look down on them.
rows.anchor: وزيادة في كرب أهل النار بأن شرفوا عليهم وبخلق إدراك أهل النار لذلك النداء

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He says the saved speak out of joy and gloating, further grieving the damned, while the account benefits listeners as a moral lesson.
rows.anchor: اغتباطا بحالهم وشماتة بأهل النار وزيادة في غمهم وليكون حكايته لطفا لمن سمعها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The caller between the groups is an angel commanded by God, who announces that God's curse is upon wrongdoers.
rows.anchor: وهو ملك يأمره الله تعالى فينادي بينهم يسمع أهل الجنة وأهل النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The saved state explicitly what God promised them; the damned ask about everything promised to both groups, confirming it and regretting the believers' reward.
rows.anchor: فهل وجدتم ما وعد ربكم حقا قالوا نعم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question may omit the object “you,” recoverable from the preceding words; the saved mention their promised reward while the question encompasses every afterlife promise.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون حذف المفعول الذي للخطاب لدلالة ما قبله عليه

rows.speaker: ابن وثاب والأعمش والكسائي
rows.claim: They read “yes” with a kasra on the ʿayn; “that” may introduce an explanation or be a softened form of the emphatic particle, which most aptly takes qad before a finite verb.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن وثاب والأعمش والكسائي نعم بكسر العين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gabriel is identified as the announcer because he makes both groups hear the news; another report says it was a different, unspecified angel.
rows.anchor: جبريل يسمع الفريقين تفريحا وتبريحا، وقيل: ملك غيره معين

rows.speaker: طاوس
rows.claim: When Ṭāwūs warned Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik of the “day of announcement,” he cited this verse; Hishām fainted, and Ṭāwūs contrasted descriptive humiliation with seeing it directly.
rows.anchor: يوم فأذن مؤذن الآية فصعق هشام فقال طاوس هذا ذل الصفة فكيف ذل المعاينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Between them” can be the adverb governed by “announced” or an adjective for the announcer with an omitted governing word.
rows.anchor: وبينهم يحتمل أن يكون معمولا لأذن ويحتمل أن يكون صفة لمؤذن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamza, al-Kisāʾī, Ibn ʿĀmir, and al-Bazzī read emphatic “that” with accusative curse; ʿĀṣim's reading from al-Aʿmash has a kasra and may quote or make “announced” mean “said.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأخوان وابن عامر والبزي أن لعنة الله بتثقيل أن ونصب لعنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The remaining seven readers use a light softened or explanatory particle and nominative “curse.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ باقي السبعة إن يفتح الهمزة خفيفة النون ورفع لعنة على الابتداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description of wrongdoers refers to their former habit of obstructing God's path and distorting it; here “wrongdoers” are unbelievers, since the text says they disbelieve in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: لأن الفاسق ليس كافرا بالآخرة بل مؤمن مصدق بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The barrier is between the two groups, as the rational plural pronoun “between them” indicates; another view puts it between Paradise and Hell, identified with the wall in 57:13.
rows.anchor: وبينهما حجاب أي بين الفريقين لأنهم المحدث عنهم وهو الظاهر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He identifies the barrier with the wall separating Paradise and Hell.
rows.anchor: وقالَه ابن عباس: ويقوي أنه بين الفريقين لفظ بينهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The barrier's location does not preclude the wall lying between elevated Paradise and the lowest Fire.
rows.anchor: ولا يحيل ضرب السور بعد ما بين الجنة والنار وإن كانت تلك في السماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Men on the barrier's heights recognize both groups by God-given marks, such as white or black faces or other signs He inspires them to know.
rows.anchor: يعرفون كلا من فريقي الجنة والنار بعلامتهم التي ميزهم الله بها من ابيضاض وجوه واسوداد وجوه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās calls the Heights a hill between Paradise and Hell; Mujāhid calls it a barrier.
rows.anchor: والأعراف تل بين الجنة والنار

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He says the Heights are the upper parts of the wall between Paradise and Hell.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أعالي السور الذي ضرب بين الجنة والنار قاله الزمخشري

rows.speaker: جابر عن رسول الله
rows.claim: A report from Jabir, transmitting from the Prophet, says those whose good and bad deeds balance are people of the Heights who have not entered but hope to.
rows.anchor: وروي في مسند ابن أبي خيثمة عن جابر عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم حديث فيه قيل يا رسول الله

rows.speaker: حذيفة بن اليمان
rows.claim: He also calls them people whose minor sins delayed them until the last arrivals.
rows.anchor: قال حذيفة بن اليمان أيضا هم قوم أبطأت بهم صغائرهم إلى آخر الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other reports identify them as warriors killed without parental permission, children with only one parent's approval, children born outside marriage, children of polytheists, prisoners who kept their religion, or scholars troubled about livelihood.
rows.anchor: وقيل غزاة جاهدوا من غير إذن والديهم فقتلوا في المعركة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He calls them late-entering Muslims whose limited works leave them awaiting God's decree between Paradise and Hell.
rows.anchor: رجال من المسلمين من آخرهم دخولا في الجنة لقصور أعمالهم

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: He says the verse requires only that people of Paradise delayed in entering stand on high ground, observe both groups, and recognize good and evil by their marks.
rows.anchor: واللازم من الآية أن على أعراف ذلك السور أو على مواضع مرتفعة عن الفريقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He finds the balanced-deeds interpretation best supported by Jabir's report and several Companions, while the other specific identifications lack clear evidence.
rows.anchor: والأقوال السابقة تحتاج إلى دليل واضح في التخصيص والجيد منها هو الأول لحديث جابر

rows.speaker: أمية بن الصلت
rows.claim: His verse portrays others on the Heights hoping for a Paradise adorned with pomegranates and greenery.
rows.anchor: وفي شعر أمية بن الصلت: وآخرون على الأعراف قد طمعوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other locations proposed for the Heights are the bridge, a spot on the bridge, or a mountain in or above Paradise; its men are variously called angels, virtuous scholars, martyrs, named Companions, or prophets.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم: إنه الصراط، وقيل: موضع على الصراط

rows.speaker: مجاهد والحسن
rows.claim: They identify the people as the most virtuous believers and scholars; another view says martyrs, preferred by al-Naḥḥās, with a report naming Ḥamza, al-ʿAbbās, ʿAlī, and Jaʿfar.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد والحسن هم فضلاء المؤمنين وعلماؤهم

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود وابن عباس وحذيفة وأبو هريرة
rows.claim: These Companions also identify the people of the Heights as those whose good and bad deeds balance.
rows.anchor: وقالَه ابن مسعود وابن عباس وحذيفة وأبو هريرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronouns in the following speech refer to the people standing on the Heights, which rules out identifying them as prophets or residents of a mountain within Paradise.
rows.anchor: الظاهر أن الضمير في ونادوا إلى آخر الآية عائد على الرجال الذين على الأعراف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects the elaborate account that they temporarily sat in elevated places to watch both groups before being moved to Paradise; “not entered it” means not yet in their assigned homes.
rows.anchor: وفي غاية البعد ما تؤول من ذلك ليصح شيء من تلك الأقوال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here “they hope” means certainty, as in Abraham's confidence that God can forgive him; a poem also uses “hope” with certainty.
rows.anchor: وقد جاء الطمع بمعنى اليقين قال والذي أطمع أن يغفر لي خطيئتي يوم الدين

rows.speaker: القاضي والجبائي
rows.claim: They reject a mountain of the Heights because entry to Paradise implies deserving it, and because an elevated seat over both groups would honor people with balanced deeds too much.
rows.anchor: فقد طعن فيه القاضي والجبائي وقالا: هو فاسد لأن قوله بما كنتم تعلمون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reply says the address may concern a particular group, not everyone in Paradise; their position could be an intermediate rank rather than an honor.
rows.anchor: وأجيب بأنه يحتمل أن يكون ونودوا خطاب مع أقوام معينين فلا يلزم أن تكون أهل الجنة كذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The words “they did not enter it” may describe the people of Paradise as the men of the Heights call to them, while “they hope” independently reports the Heights' expectation; another reading makes not entering a state of the callers.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المعنى ونادى أصحاب الأعراف أصحاب الجنة بالسلام وهم قد دخلوا الجنة

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود وقتادة والسدي
rows.claim: They take the call as directed to people already in Paradise, while the people of the Heights themselves have not entered; Ibn Masʿūd says God put this hope in their hearts for a good end.
rows.anchor: وهذا تأويل ابن مسعود وقتادة والسدي وغيرهم، وقال ابن مسعود: والله ما جعل الله

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: He also says their hope remained because the light in their hands did not go out when the hypocrites' light went dark.
rows.anchor: إنما طمع أصحاب الأعراف لأن النور الذي كان في أيديهم لم يطفأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation says they did not enter while hopeful, but were instead in fear and despair until God's pardon reached them.
rows.anchor: لم يدخلوها في حال طمع لها بل كانوا في حال يأس وخوف

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He treats “they have not entered, while hoping” as a new sentence answering why they have not entered: they are detained but still hopeful; it may also modify an antecedent.
rows.anchor: لا محل له لأنه استئناف كأن سائلا سأل عن أصحاب الأعراف فقيل له لم يدخلوها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He calls that syntactic explanation weak because a clause separates the alleged adjective from its noun without functioning as a parenthesis.
rows.anchor: وهذا توجيه ضعيف للفصل بين الموصوف وصفته بجملة ونادوا وليست جملة اعتراض

rows.speaker: ابن النحوي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Naḥwī reads “they are expectant.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن النحوي وهم طامعون

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وجماعة
rows.claim: They take the eyes as belonging to the people of the Heights: they greet Paradise's people, then look toward Hell and ask God not to place them there.
rows.anchor: والضمير في أبصارهم عائد على رجال الأعراف يسلمون على أهل الجنة

rows.speaker: أبو مجلز
rows.claim: He instead assigns the eyes to people of Paradise who had not entered yet.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو مجلز: الضمير لأهل الجنة وهم لم يدخلوها بعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording suggests they usually look toward Paradise and are involuntarily made to turn toward Hell; its terrifying sight drives them to plead for mercy, invoking God as their caring Lord.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله صرفت دليل أن أكثر أحوالهم النظر إلى تلقاء أصحاب الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Heights' call may address men already in Hell, whom they recognize by familiar marks or blackened faces; Abū Mujliz says angels speak, while most identify the Heights' people as humans.
rows.anchor: يحتمل أن يكون هذا النداء وأولئك الرجال في النار ومعرفتهم إياهم في الدنيا بعلامات

rows.speaker: ابن القشيري
rows.claim: He names the arrogant leaders they recognize—al-Walīd, Abū Jahl, al-ʿĀṣ, ʿUqba, Umayya, Ubayy, and other chiefs—and their worldly wealth, children, troops, guards, and armies.
rows.anchor: يا وليد بن المغيرة يا أبا جهل بن هشام يا عاصي بن وائل يا عتبة بن أبي معيط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question about their gathering is a rebuke; “what you used to be arrogant about” may be a nominalized source phrase, and some read a verb meaning “amass” instead.
rows.anchor: وما أغنى استفهام توبيخ وتقريع، وقيل: نافية

rows.speaker: إياد بن لقيط
rows.claim: Iyād ibn Luqayṭ reads “they are resentful.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ إياد بن لقيط وهم ساخطون

rows.speaker: الأعمش
rows.claim: Al-Aʿmash reads “when their eyes were turned.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعمش وإذا قلبت أبصارهم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He takes “Are these the ones?” as a reference to poor believers whom worldly leaders looked down on and swore would receive no divine mercy; they are now told to enter Paradise.
rows.anchor: الإشارة إلى أهل الجنة الذين كان الرؤساء يستهينون بهم ويحقرونهم لفقرهم وقلة حظوظهم في الدنيا

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: He transmits the same interpretation from some exegetes: the despised weak were sworn to be excluded, yet are ordered into Paradise.
rows.anchor: وذكره ابن عطية عن بعض المتأولين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He says an angel, acting by God's command, points to the people of the Heights while addressing the people of Hell.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: أهؤلاء من كلام ملك بأمر الله إشارة إلى أهل الأعراف

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: He says the people of Hell had sworn that the Heights' people would join them in Hell; angels challenge them with the pointed question, after the Heights rebuked them.
rows.anchor: قال النقاش لما وبخوهم بقولهم ما أغنى عنكم جمعكم أقسم أهل النار أن أهل الأعراف داخلون النار

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: He takes the referent as the people of the Heights and the speakers as themselves, turning to one another with the command to enter Paradise.
rows.anchor: فيقول بعضهم لبعض ادخلوا الجنة قاله الحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other views point to believers the pagans swore would not enter Paradise, with God or angels speaking, or make the speaker Mālik, keeper of Hell; Abū Mujliz makes the Heights' people angels pointing to Paradise's people.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الإشارة إلى المؤمنين الذين كان الكفار يحلفون أنهم لا يدخلون الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readings include causative “let them enter,” past “they entered,” or passive “they were admitted”; with the latter readings, “no fear” is spoken to them.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وابن هرمز: أدخلوا من أدخل أي أدخلوا أنفسكم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He says the people of the Heights enter after watching both groups, demonstrating that reward follows deeds and urging listeners to outdo one another in good works.
rows.anchor: وفائدة ذلك بيان أن الجزاء على قدر الأعمال وأن التقدم والتأخر على حسبها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He dismisses this as rhetorical over-elaboration without benefit and detects a Muʿtazilite implication.
rows.anchor: وهو تكثير من باب الخطابة لا طائل تحته وفيه دسيسة الاعتزال
